title: AI-Driven and Automated Continuous Oxygen Saturation Monitoring and LTOT: A Systematic Review
abstract: Abstract Background Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) is essential for patients with chronic hypoxemia, particularly due to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). However, conventional LTOT relies on static oxygen flow rates that fail to reflect patients’ fluctuating physiological demands. Emerging systems leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) and automation offer real-time SpO₂ monitoring and adaptive oxygen titration. This systematic review evaluates the performance, usability, and clinical readiness of such technologies in LTOT. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus (2000–2024) for English-language, peer-reviewed studies describing AI or automated SpO₂ systems in adults with LTOT relevance. Inclusion criteria focused on systems addressing motion artifacts, low-perfusion reliability, or skin tone bias. Extracted data included algorithm design, accuracy (e.g., MAE, RMSE), usability, and risk of bias. Results Eight studies met the inclusion criteria: five AI-based and three automated systems. AI models achieved high SpO₂ estimation accuracy (MAE as low as 0.57%) and addressed motion artifacts and demographic bias. Cabanas et al. 6 notably performed skin tone–stratified validation. Automated systems like O₂matic and iPOC demonstrated clinical efficacy in maintaining SpO₂ targets and reducing provider workload. However, AI models were mostly in prototype or simulation stages and lacked real-world LTOT validation. Risk of bias was moderate to high, especially in participant selection and algorithm transparency. Conclusions AI and automation offer distinct yet synergistic benefits for modernizing LTOT. Automated systems support immediate clinical use, while AI models hold promise for personalized, predictive oxygen therapy. Future work must prioritize real-world validation, equity, usability, and regulatory alignment to ensure ethical and effective integration into LTOT care.

title: Blockchain-Based Dynamic and Revocable Consent for Secondary Health Data Use: Systematic Review
abstract: Background: The secondary use of health data holds substantial potential for advancing biomedical research, strengthening population health analytics, and enabling artificial intelligence-driven decision-making support. Yet, ensuring that such reuse respects patient autonomy, privacy, and regulatory obligations remains a major challenge. Conventional consent mechanisms are typically static, difficult to revoke, and offer limited transparency or accountability after data disclosure. Objective: This review aimed to systematically examine blockchain-based frameworks that enable dynamic, auditable, and revocable consent for the secondary use of health data. Methods: A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science covering the period 2020 to 2025. Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, 55 peer-reviewed studies meeting predefined inclusion criteria were analyzed. Data extraction focused on four dimensions: (1) consent life cycle management, (2) auditability and traceability, (3) usability and patient empowerment, and (4) legal and ethical alignment. Results: Findings indicate that blockchain technologies provide a robust foundation for automating consent life cycles, ensuring immutable auditability, and enabling decentralized patient control. Most frameworks used smart contracts, decentralized identifiers, and verifiable credentials to implement programmable and verifiable consent processes. Nevertheless, key challenges persist, including limited usability testing, complexities in real-time revocation propagation, interoperability gaps with clinical systems, and tensions with regulatory requirements such as the General Data Protection Regulation right to erasure. Only a small subset of studies reported real-world deployments or user-centered evaluations. Conclusions: Blockchain offers substantial promise for improving the trustworthiness, transparency, and accountability of consent management for secondary health data use. However, wider adoption requires human-centered design approaches, stronger interoperability through standards such as Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, verifiable credentials, and consent receipts, and clearer legal guidance for compliance. Future research should prioritize integrating blockchain-enabled consent infrastructures into national and cross-border digital health ecosystems such as the European Health Data Space to support secure, patient-controlled, and ethically governed secondary data use.

title: Innovative teaching and learning
abstract: The rapid advancement of technology, globalization, and the evolving demands of society have transformed the landscape of education, leading to the emergence of innovative pedagogical models that emphasize learner-centred, competency-oriented, and experiential approaches to teaching and learning. Traditional education, which primarily focused on teacher-centred instruction and memorization of knowledge, is gradually being replaced by instructional models that promote critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, communication, problem-solving, and lifelong learning. Future pedagogical models aim to prepare learners not only for academic success but also for active participation in an increasingly complex, technology-driven, and knowledge-based global society.Future pedagogical models recognize that learning is a dynamic, continuous, and individualized process. Students differ in their learning styles, abilities, interests, experiences, and career aspirations. Consequently, modern educational approaches encourage flexible learning pathways, personalized instruction, collaborative learning environments, authentic assessment, and real-world problem-solving experiences. These models emphasize active learner participation, enabling students to construct knowledge through inquiry, exploration, experimentation, reflection, and meaningful engagement with educational content.Digital transformation has significantly influenced the development of future pedagogical models. Technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), Learning Management Systems (LMS), cloud computing, learning analytics, virtual and augmented reality, mobile learning, and intelligent educational platforms provide opportunities for personalized instruction, adaptive learning, immediate feedback, and continuous assessment. These technological innovations support educators in designing engaging learning experiences while enabling students to access educational resources anytime and anywhere. Technology therefore serves as an important enabler of innovative pedagogical practices that promote educational accessibility, flexibility, and inclusiveness.Future pedagogical models also emphasize the development of competencies rather than the mere acquisition of factual knowledge. Educational institutions increasingly focus on measurable learning outcomes, practical skills, ethical values, digital competencies, leadership abilities, creativity, innovation, and interdisciplinary thinking. Learners are encouraged to apply theoretical concepts in authentic situations, collaborate with peers, solve real-world problems, and continuously reflect upon their own learning experiences. Such competency-oriented approaches prepare graduates for higher education, professional careers, entrepreneurship, and lifelong learning.Collaboration and active participation are central characteristics of modern pedagogical models. Rather than functioning as passive recipients of information, students become active contributors to the learning process through discussions, projects, investigations, simulations, case studies, and collaborative problem-solving activities. Educators assume the role of facilitators, mentors, and learning designers who guide students in developing independent thinking, analytical reasoning, communication skills, and professional competencies. This transformation strengthens learner engagement while fostering intellectual curiosity and self-directed learning.Future pedagogical models also promote educational inclusiveness and learner diversity. Personalized instruction, adaptive learning technologies, differentiated teaching strategies, and flexible assessment methods ensure that learners with diverse backgrounds, abilities, and educational needs receive appropriate academic support. Inclusive learning environments encourage equal participation, reduce learning barriers, and provide equitable educational opportunities for all students regardless of their social, cultural, linguistic, or physical characteristics.Educational institutions increasingly recognize that future learning extends beyond traditional classroom boundaries. Community engagement, industry collaboration, internships, service learning, research projects, virtual learning environments, and experiential activities provide authentic learning opportunities that connect academic knowledge with practical application. Such experiences enable students to develop professional competencies, social responsibility, leadership qualities, and adaptability required for success in rapidly changing global environments.Despite their numerous advantages, the implementation of future pedagogical models presents several challenges. Educational institutions require curriculum redesign, teacher professional development, technological infrastructure, effective assessment strategies, institutional support, and continuous quality assurance to successfully adopt innovative teaching practices. Educators must also develop the pedagogical knowledge and digital competencies necessary to integrate emerging technologies with learner-centred instructional approaches while maintaining educational quality and academic integrity.As education continues to evolve, future pedagogical models are expected to become increasingly integrated with Artificial Intelligence, learning analytics, immersive technologies, competency-based assessment, adaptive learning systems, and global digital learning networks. These developments will contribute to more personalized, collaborative, flexible, and competency-oriented educational environments that prepare learners for the opportunities and challenges of the twenty-first century.This chapter explores six important future pedagogical models: Competency-Based Learning, Inquiry-Based Learning, Project-Based Learning, Problem-Based Learning, Personalized Learning, and Experiential Learning. Together, these approaches illustrate how innovative teaching methodologies are reshaping education to develop knowledgeable, skilled, creative, and lifelong learners capable of thriving in an interconnected and rapidly changing world.

title: Prevalence of Self-Diagnosis among Nepalese College Students
abstract: Practice of diagnosing oneself with medical condition or disorder without confirmation by official diagnostician through the usage of various symptoms checker websites, assurance from one’s sources, books, magazines; apps and artificial intelligence chatbots to diagnose oneself with doubted medical condition, acute or chronic comes under self-diagnosis. This study determined the prevalence of self-diagnosis among Nepalese college students, was to examine the self-diagnosis habits and attitude of the students towards self-diagnosis in the absence of a registered doctor, physician or psychiatrist. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among N=408 college students of Kathmandu valley. A google form was designed with both close ended and open-ended questions to collect data. SPSS v20 was used to develop data file and descriptive statistical tools are used to analyze the collected data. Weighted average mean was calculated to develop attitude variable with four five-point Likert scale items. The study revealed that majority of Nepalese college students (76.5%) use Google as their main search engine for self-diagnosis. Friends and family members are the option of Nepalese students for self-diagnosis of their illness. The finding of the study suggested that most of Nepalese college students (66.7%) have doubt on accuracy of self-diagnosis through internet. The result of the study portrays that there is positive attitude towards self- diagnosis. Accuracy of self-diagnosis is still questionable, so self-diagnosis practice should be discouraged as sometimes it may provide false assurance to severe cases through mis-diagnosis. The positive attitude towards self-diagnosis among them indicates the future scope of internet of things in self-diagnosis. Accuracy of self-diagnosis is still questionable, so self-diagnosis practice should be discouraged as sometimes it may provide false assurance to severe cases through mis-diagnosis. The study identified limited evidence on the diagnostic accuracy of self-diagnosis. Awareness regarding negative impact of self-diagnosis and symptoms checking habits is necessary. Health literacy among the Nepalese people is essential, the study contributes in the literature of self-diagnosis. Policy makers should be aware towards discouraging self-diagnosing habits among Nepalese people.

title: Unleashing Effective Models of Collaboration for Rainwater Harvesting: Experiences from Nepal
abstract: Background: Rainwater harvesting (RWH) is an age-old practice of a localized renewable and alternate source of water supply to meet the growing demand of people in developing countries like Nepal. Thus, the effective models of collaboration for providing water services through RWH is a pathway to the sustainable water management of the nation leading to achieving SDGs. Purpose: The paper aims at unleashing effective models of collaboration for RWH in the context of the rural areas of Nepal. Methodology: The study comprises a descriptive cum analytical research design based on both primary and secondary data. The necessary primary data were collected by conducting a field survey using a semi-structured questionnaire on a sample of 38 communities/projects having RWH systems while the secondary data were collected through relevant publications. The csollected data were analyzed using statistical tools through SPSS to derive results leading to major findings of the study. Analysis/Results: The study concluded that a collaborative plan provides a ground to get contributions from different stakeholders and increase their sense of ownership. The collaboration with the local government ensures co-financing and involvement in planning and monitoring and increases prospects for support to required rehabilitation in the future. Community engagement from planning to implementation to managing the systems ensures the system's functionality and sustainability, leading to caretakers’ management and promoting income-generating activities using waste/overflow water from the system. The multiple uses of water services (MUS) provide a basis for livelihood enhancement leading to regular payment of tariffs. The caretakers’ management ensures to fix minor repairs promptly as needed. A combination of monitoring and eval_uation with different stakeholders during implementation and afterward ensures efficient and effective implementation and sustainability of the RWH system. Originality/Value: No such study uses recent data related to effective models of collaboration for RWH in the context of the rural areas of developing countries like Nepal is accessible. The paper, therefore, is valuable for users’ committees, development actors, academia, and policymakers to create effective models of collaboration for RWH. This work may potentially be useful to academia for future studies. Future avenue: The extension of this study can be made by incorporating an analysis of diverse applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in the water management sector in future studies.

title: Skin tones and stereotypes: racial inequity in medical beauty norms
abstract: To the Editor, Cosmetic surgery and dermatology are two fields that deal with both health and beauty. They have a big impact on how people see normalcy and what they want. So, it’s very important that we pay close attention to the health standards of beauty. It is increasingly likely that these standards are predominantly based on Eurocentric notions. This not only promotes racial bias but it also has real, negative effects on patient care and health equity. This article is compliant with the TITAN Guidelines 2025 governing the declaration and use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in research and publication[1] One big problem is that medical school hasn’t always had a lot of different kinds of people, especially in dermatology. For a long time, books and hands-on classes in dermatology have mostly been about skin problems that affect White people. This is a big lack of information because many diseases look different on people of color. This means that Black, Asian, and other non-White people get the wrong diagnosis, get treatment later, and have worse health outcomes. This isn’t about how it looks; it’s about having the right skills and keeping people safe[2,3]. There is also a clear bias in cosmetic surgery, which is usually done to make White people look better. Messages that say things like “smaller noses,” “thinner lips,” or “certain forehead shapes” might slowly push people of different races to conform to a single, limiting standard of beauty. It’s important to respect the patient’s right to privacy, but the business needs to think about whether it’s just meeting demand or intentionally making it in a way that devalues racial features and supports a racial hierarchy of beauty[4]. This absurd demand affects not merely how well a medical professional does what they do, additionally how mentally fit their clients are. If the profession of medicine decides what is “standard” or “perfect,” with no taking race into account, Black people may feel like they don’t belong or are not sufficient. Individuals might start loosing faith in the medical sector and view their distinctive qualities as issues requiring rectification rather than attributes to take pride in[5]. In short, the medical field needs to work hard to get rid of the Eurocentric beauty standards that many of its methods are based on right now. We need to work together to make sure that training materials are more diverse, that clinical research includes people from all walks of life, and that beauty medicine promotes a culture that values and enhances a wide range of ethnic traits. Everyone should be involved in real patient care, and it shouldn’t push a certain, biased idea. Instead, it should celebrate how different people look.

title: Plagiarism and AI Content
abstract: The word plagiarize comes from Latin word plagiarius that means a kidnaper. The word plagiary, a derivative of plagiarus was introduced in English in 1601 to describe someone guilty of literary theft.1 The World Association of Medical Editors (WAME)2 defines plagiarism as “the use of other’s published and unpublished ideas or words (or other intellectual property) without attribution or permission and presenting them as new and original rather than derived from an existing source.” Plagiarism is considered to be a serious crime of academia. The incidence of plagiarism is common and depends on the field of research as well as the researcher. On a study done by international journal of exercise science to see plagiarism in the submitted manuscript, they found that 46% of the manuscript submitted have contained some form of plagiarism.3 Why plagiarism is high? Some of the reasons are every academician has a hidden desire to publish, writing has been made mandatory by some medical institutions. So there is a compulsion to publish, or perish. But there is lack of time, research skill and ease of obtaining articles from internet. Another reason is misbelief that taking paragraphs from different papers is accepted as the references are mentioned but this results in copy-cut-paste which is plagiarism. Plagiarism free writing is a shared responsibility among the writer, expert and the institution. To avoid plagiarism, the author should provide references, use of quotation mark if exact word or sentence to be copied followed by credit the source, use of software, take guidance from the seniors. Currently the intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and plagiarism has become an important issue in the field of research. It raises important question about authorship, originality and ethical consideration when AI content generating tools are used. AI generated content has complicated the definition of plagiarism. Generative AI has facilitated the generation of ideas and drafting of complete text. One of the key criteria for authorship is accountability for every aspects of work (research writing). Hence generative AI cannot be considered as an author as they cannot be held responsible for the integrity and originality of work. The ethical practical challenges of AI generated contents lie in their accuracy and reliability, there is no authorship, hallucinations and errors i.e. AI can fabricate data, citations requiring verifications. The author should disclose the use of AI in their research. Currently there is no clear consensus on the standard use of AI in academic medicines. However some guidelines are proposed by international Committee of Medical Journal Editors.4 Plagiarism in manuscript writing is a huge problem and to eliminate it, is a challenge. It’s a common responsibility of all the stakeholders to make a plagiarism free writing. Author should be aware of plagiarism and take all the responsibility to avoid plagiarism.

title: AI and Learning: A Management Perspective from College Students of Kathmandu Valley, Nepal
abstract: Background: With the quick integration of Artificial Intelligence in the global education system, it is quite essential that the impact of AI on student learning be determined. Although the studies have started in Nepal, a large gap is still present within the framework of student perceptions towards the influence of AI on learning. Objectives: The objectives of this research were to examine the perceived effect of AI on the learning outcomes of college-going youth in the Kathmandu Valley, as well as to identify if the effect is considerably different for the chosen demographic: gender, age, and discipline. Methods: In the current study, a quantitative, cross-sectional survey was administered to 319 college students using convenience sampling. The core instrument measured perceived impact across six dimensions (learning effectiveness, outcome quality, memory retention, motivation, anxiety, and analytical skills) using a 7-point Likert scale combined into a composite dependent variable. Data analysis was done through descriptive statistics, testing the reliability of the scales using Cronbach's alpha, and independent sample t-test and one-way ANOVA analyses to test for mean differences across demographic groups. Results: The overall aggregate result for the composite score (4.74 out of 7) reflected a mildly positive yet neutral-leaning attitude regarding AI's influence. The reliability analysis corroborated internal consistency for the overall composite scale. More importantly, the results for ANOVA tests did not yield any statistically significant differences for mean composite scores in any of the gender (p=.882), age (p=.344), or fields of study (p=.269) groups. Although some slight shifts did occur in certain descriptive groups (notably Health & Welfare students had the highest mean value), none actually proved statistically significant. Conclusion: Results provide strong evidence for the existence of a certain consensus among college students in Kathmandu Valley on the integrated effects of AI on learning experiences, which do not seem to be confined within the usual demographic constraints. This sends out a strong signal for emerging approaches toward the integration of AI in education to not be demographically nuanced. However, the absence of significant differences points toward factors other than demographic differences becoming significantly crucial in influencing students’ perceptions. Novelty: Being one of the first studies to empirically investigate in the Nepalese setting beyond access and general attitudes to explore the perceived effects of AI on the multi-dimensional construct of learning outcomes, the methodical approach through the use of composite measurement and demographic analysis contributes to the local literature’s refinement.

title: Reimagining rehabilitation in Christianson syndrome: can virtual reality bridge the gap?
abstract: To the Editor, Christianson syndrome (CS) is a rare autosomal recessive X-linked disorder with a mutation in the SLC9A6 gene, exhibited mainly in males with females as carriers. It is represented by intellectual disability, developmental delay, and regression. The clinical presentation of CS comprises autism or Angelman syndrome characteristics, microcephaly, sensory deficits, craniofacial dysmorphism, ataxia, absent verbal communication, seizures (epilepsy), low weight, height, and oculomotor palsy with reduced life span. The treatment plan for CS does not depend solely on medications, but effective rehabilitation training is a more significant symptomatic and supportive approach[1]. Virtual Reality (VR) therapy is one of the emerging and optimistic treatment approaches for neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, various postural control disorders, and mobility disorders. It provides high-intensity, repetitive visual, auditory, motor, and somatosensory stimuli to interact with cognitive, motor, and sensory functions, offering individuals’ feedback to sense their own body position and movement directions. This is based on visual tracking and an interactive environment reproducing the surrounding reality to coordinate their body position[2,3]. Incorporation of sensory feedback, such as spatial audio and haptic feedback, enhances the feeling of an actual real surrounding in the virtual reality, further supporting rehabilitation[3]. Globally, 2.5 million individuals have been reported to suffer from multiple sclerosis (MS). A 40-participant trial showed significant improvement of neurological functions for 19 individuals in the VR group compared to the non-VR group[3]. The symptoms of MS often coincide with CS, highlighting the advancement of VR therapy. A study revealed that a patient 2 years poststroke exhibited improved sensorimotor functions using a PS2 EyeToy, a low-cost VR device. This demonstrates that low-cost VR devices can provide convenient home-based rehabilitation[4]. Since sensorimotor dysfunction is seen in CS, applying VR technology should improve the sensory deficits. A 12-week VR program improved proprioception while maintaining balance in patients with Parkinson’s disease[2]. Additionally, a cohort study of 16 healthy older adults showed that prompt gamma sensory stimulation via VR technology affects various sensory modalities[5]. Despite all these advancements, the validity of VR programs is yet to be explored because of the highly expensive technologies that require great expertise to employ them. It is not fully confirmed if the virtual world experiences actually transfer to an individual’s daily habits and life. The social and societal acceptance of the VR devices’ usage is also crucial to create a safe environment for pupils to rehabilitate. Another challenge revolves around the heterogeneous nature of neurological disorders, which makes it difficult to perform homogeneous trials on patients, even if a much smaller group is considered. It may be addressed by the personalized phenotypic interventional approach that again requires a highly skilled healthcare team to give an individual treatment plan[6]. As the burden of neurological diseases is increasing worldwide, it is necessary to address the rising sensorimotor disability by incorporating advanced rehabilitation. VR Therapy is changing the future of disability because of its real-life-based virtual reality, where patient engagement is optimal. So, for this purpose, research-based trials should be prioritized in order to learn VR therapy effectiveness, cost cost-effective programs with a skilled workforce must be started[2,6]. The need for interdisciplinary approaches between artificial intelligence and medicine would help healthcare providers better understand the application of these fields[6]. This highlights the need for integrated schemes and strategies between policymakers and healthcare professionals for further interventional investigations. The focus of the current research on CS has mostly been on its genetic basis and its symptomatic treatment through traditional rehabilitation[1]. However, similar neurological conditions highlighting the potential of using technological innovations in these aspects have also been pointed out by recent studies[2,3]. Sensory-motor integration and quality of life, in general, could be improved via such technologies. One can make a connection between the CS symptoms, notably ataxia, loss of sensation, and behavioral regression, and the positive effects of VR on patients with similar problems in MS[3], Parkinson’s disease[2], or even Post-stroke[4] rehabilitation, thus shedding light on the ways of overcoming the insufficient support therapies for rare X-linked disorders. To move forward in this direction, it is essential to conduct large-scale randomized controlled trials assessing the effectiveness of VR in CS patients, create affordable VR programs that can be used at home with little training, and establish collaborations among neuroscientists, technologists, and policymakers to make individual VR treatment a part of the clinical guidelines[6]. This will not only improve the quality of life of such patients but also lead to a breakthrough in the field of rehabilitation. In conclusion, VR-based therapy represents an emerging and potentially transformative modality in the management and rehabilitation of neurological disorders. Future efforts should focus on the establishment of standardized clinical protocols, the conduct of large-scale randomized controlled trials, and the integration of VR interventions into evidence-based clinical practice. These strategies are essential to validate efficacy, ensure safety, and optimize patient-centered outcomes, ultimately contributing to improved quality of life among neurological patient populations. This letter to the editor adheres to the Transparency in the Reporting of Artificial Intelligence in Research (TITAN) guideline[7].

title: Addressing the psychological burden: the case for resilience in medical training
abstract: To the Editor, A lot of people know about the problem in Pakistan, but not many people talk about it: medical students are under a lot of psychological stress. The hard classes, fierce rivalry, and high expectations from society all make academic stress common and even required for success. Because of this, we need to look more closely at the psychological features we search for in medical students. People often admire attributes like grit, but in a circumstance like this, where the stakes are great, their significance may be more complicated than we believe. This means we need to put more effort into making students stronger so that they can defend their health and the healthcare system in the long run. This article is compliant with the TITAN Guidelines 2025 governing the declaration and use of artificial intelligence tools in research and publication[1]. People frequently argue that having “grit,” which is having the desire and tenacity to reach long-term goals, is a key to success. But when it comes to medical education in Pakistan, putting too much emphasis on grit could have bad outcomes that weren’t meant to happen. Gritty students may set very high goals for themselves and keep going through pain and fatigue until they reach the point of burnout. This relentless desire, together with not having adequate skills to deal with stress, can make mental stress worse. New studies reveal that grit can help people accomplish well, but it doesn’t necessarily keep them from getting hurt mentally in a stressful situation. It can even be linked to unhealthy perfectionism at times[2]. On the other hand, resilience seems to be a more crucial feature that protects people. This means being able to change and get back on your feet after hard times. It’s not enough to only get through hard times; you also have to do it successfully. For medical students, this involves learning how to handle stress, keep things in perspective, and ask for support when they need it. Studies have shown time and time again that trainees who are more resilient feel less stressed and do better mentally when they are under a lot of academic and clinical strain[3]. We shouldn’t strive to help students deal with stress better. Instead, we should try to make them stronger so they can deal with it in a good way. It’s also vital to know that stress doesn’t affect everyone in the same way. Studies generally find that girls and students in their first and third years of school, which are transitional years, feel more academic stress. This suggests that there are institutional and curricular issues that make things harder for some groups[4]. This suggests that the organization has to make adjustments instead of merely telling the kid to “be tougher.” Some examples of interventions that have been demonstrated to relieve stress and promote well-being in similar contexts are mindfulness training, peer support groups, and mental health facilities that are easy to go to[5]. In the end, we want Pakistan to change how it teaches medicine. It’s crucial to accomplish well in school and keep going, but not if it hurts your mental health. Medical schools ought to stop rewarding people for putting up with suffering and instead encourage people to be strong. By combining research-based wellness programs with a supportive learning environment, we can make sure that we are producing doctors who are not only competent but also healthy, strong, and caring for future generations.

title: Digital transformation in education
abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed the educational landscape, giving rise to digital learning ecosystems that integrate technology, pedagogy, and educational resources to create flexible, interactive, and learner-centred learning environments. Digital learning ecosystems consist of interconnected digital tools, platforms, technologies, educational content, teachers, learners, and institutional support systems that work together to enhance teaching, learning, assessment, communication, and educational management. These ecosystems have become essential components of modern education, enabling institutions to deliver high-quality learning experiences that are accessible, inclusive, and adaptable to the changing needs of society.The evolution of digital technologies has significantly changed the traditional classroom model. Educational institutions now utilize digital classrooms, learning management systems, cloud computing, mobile technologies, hybrid learning models, and smart learning environments to improve educational effectiveness and learner engagement. These technologies facilitate collaboration, personalized learning, real-time communication, continuous assessment, and efficient educational administration while expanding access to education beyond geographical and temporal boundaries.Digital learning ecosystems support a learner-centred approach in which students actively participate in constructing knowledge through interactive learning experiences. Teachers function as facilitators who guide learners by integrating digital resources, multimedia content, collaborative activities, and technology-enhanced instructional strategies into the learning process. This transformation encourages independent learning, critical thinking, creativity, communication, collaboration, and lifelong learning skills that are essential for success in the twenty-first century.One of the key characteristics of digital learning ecosystems is flexibility. Learners can access educational materials, participate in virtual classrooms, submit assignments, communicate with instructors, and collaborate with peers anytime and anywhere using internet-enabled devices. This flexibility supports diverse learning needs, accommodates different learning styles, and provides educational opportunities for learners who may face geographical, physical, or time-related constraints.The integration of cloud computing and mobile technologies has further strengthened digital learning ecosystems by enabling secure storage, efficient resource sharing, real-time collaboration, and continuous access to educational content. Learning management systems organize course materials, assessments, communication, and academic records, while mobile learning allows learners to engage with educational resources through smart phones, tablets, and other portable devices. These technologies collectively contribute to improving learning efficiency, accessibility, and institutional effectiveness.Hybrid learning models, which combine face-to-face instruction with online learning, have become increasingly popular in higher education and professional training. These models offer greater flexibility while maintaining meaningful interactions between teachers and learners. Smart learning environments further enhance educational experiences through the use of intelligent technologies, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, and data-driven decision-making to support personalized education and continuous improvement.Despite the numerous advantages of digital learning ecosystems, educational institutions also encounter challenges such as unequal access to technology, digital literacy gaps, cyber security concerns, infrastructure limitations, data privacy issues, and the need for continuous teacher training. Addressing these challenges requires effective educational policies, technological investment, institutional leadership, and ongoing professional development to ensure the successful implementation of digital learning initiatives.This chapter examines the major components of digital learning ecosystems through six key areas: Digital Classrooms, Learning Management Systems, Cloud-Based Education, Mobile Learning, Hybrid Learning Models, and Smart Learning Environments. Together, these topics provide a comprehensive understanding of how digital technologies are transforming teaching, learning, and educational management while preparing institutions and learners for the future of education.

title: Comment on ‘Association of Computed Tomography‐Derived Body Composition and Complications After Colorectal Cancer Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis’ by Van Helsdingen et al.
abstract: We read with great interest the article titled ‘Association of computed tomography-derived body composition and complications after colorectal cancer surgery A systematic review and meta-analysis’ and commend the authors for their rigorous and insightful systematic review and meta-analysis on body composition measurements using computed tomography (CT) scans as predictors of complications following colorectal cancer surgery [1]. This research addresses a highly relevant clinical issue, providing valuable information to guide surgical decision-making. While the article provides important findings, we believe there are some additional aspects that could further strengthen its impact and provide readers with an even more comprehensive understanding. First, although the authors conducted a thorough risk of bias assessment using the QUIPS tool, the article does not mention whether a sensitivity analysis was performed based on study quality. We suggest conducting such an analysis to examine how excluding lower-quality studies (e.g., those rated as having a high risk of bias) may impact the pooled results. Sensitivity analysis could help readers better appreciate the robustness of the findings and determine whether the conclusions are consistent across studies with varying levels of methodological rigour [2]. Second, the certainty of evidence presented in this study could have been evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) framework. GRADE is widely recognized for systematically assessing the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations in health care research. Including a GRADE assessment would allow the readers to understand the confidence in the results across different outcomes, especially given the variability in CT measurement methods and clinical endpoints considered in the studies [3]. This would also facilitate the translation of evidence into clinical practice by offering clarity on the reliability of the conclusions. Third, while the authors rightfully address the risk of publication bias in the discussion, we recommend the inclusion of formal statistical methods to assess this risk. A funnel plot or DOI plot, alongside statistical tests such as Egger's regression or the trim-and-fill method, could provide more concrete evidence of the presence or absence of publication bias [4]. These methods would further substantiate the robustness of the meta-analytic findings by ensuring that the results were not disproportionately influenced by small or positive-result studies. Furthermore, it might be valuable to explore subgroup analyses based on factors such as the specific CT measurement (e.g., visceral fat vs. sarcopenia), patient age, or cancer stage. These analyses could uncover potential variations in predictive utility across different patient populations, making the results more clinically actionable. We encourage the authors to consider the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in CT image analysis. Including a discussion on how future research could incorporate AI-based methods for body composition analysis could enhance the clinical utility of these measurements by providing more precise and automated predictors of post-surgical outcomes. We congratulate the authors for their valuable contribution to the field. By incorporating sensitivity analysis based on study quality, GRADE assessments, publication bias evaluations, and further exploration of AI-based predictive models, future work could offer even greater insights. We appreciate the opportunity to comment on this important study and look forward to future research in this area. RM, AKB, and MS critically and provided comments on methodological aspects. title: Do we adequately monitor for severe anion gap metabolic acidosis during sodium thiosulfate therapy for calciphylaxis?
abstract: Calciphylaxis is a rare but devastating disorder of vascular calcification predominantly affecting patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and is associated with extremely high morbidity and mortality. In the absence of approved disease specific therapies, sodium thiosulfate (STS) has become one of the most frequently used off-label treatments due to its calcium chelating, antioxidant, and vasodilatory properties. Contemporary reviews and expert consensus documents continue to describe STS as a central adjunctive therapy in calciphylaxis management, despite the lack of randomized controlled trial data[1]. Despite its widespread clinical use, the safety profile of STS remains incompletely defined. Metabolic acidosis, particularly high anion gap metabolic acidosis (AGMA), has been reported as an adverse effect of STS; however, severe AGMA is insufficiently emphasized and likely under-recognized in routine clinical practice. For clinical clarity, severe AGMA may be defined as arterial pH <7.20, serum bicarbonate <10 mmol/L, or acidosis necessitating treatment interruption, bicarbonate therapy, or renal replacement intervention. Observational cohorts evaluating STS therapy have reported metabolic acidosis in approximately 20–40% of treated patients, with clinically significant acidosis requiring dose modification or discontinuation occurring in nearly 5–10% of cases, highlighting a potentially underappreciated treatment related risk[2,3]. Recent systematic reviews evaluating therapeutic strategies for calciphylaxis highlight substantial heterogeneity in safety reporting related to STS. Although acid base disturbances are acknowledged, they are rarely quantified or analyzed in detail, limiting accurate risk assessment. A contemporary systematic review underscores that while STS remains widely administered, robust safety data including the incidence of clinically significant AGMA are lacking, emphasizing the need for structured pharmacovigilance[4]. Importantly, existing calciphylaxis management recommendations endorse STS use but provide limited practical guidance regarding metabolic monitoring strategies or thresholds for therapy modification, representing a critical gap between therapeutic adoption and safety oversight[1,3]. In patients with ESRD, baseline acid base homeostasis is already fragile, and the additional acid burden generated through STS metabolism to sulfate may precipitate severe metabolic derangements. STS undergoes hepatic and mitochondrial metabolism resulting in the formation of sulfate and other sulfur containing anions, contributing to accumulation of unmeasured acids and elevation of the anion gap. Impaired renal clearance in advanced kidney disease may further potentiate this acid load, predisposing patients to progressive AGMA[5]. Importantly, recent clinical guidance documents and institutional protocols caution against continued STS administration in the setting of worsening metabolic acidosis and recommend close biochemical monitoring during therapy[3]. Failure to recognize STS associated AGMA may lead to hemodynamic instability, diagnostic confusion with sepsis or uremic acidosis, and adverse clinical outcomes. In light of these observations, we propose that severe AGMA should be recognized as a clinically important and under-appreciated complication of STS therapy in calciphylaxis. Structured monitoring should be considered, including baseline assessment of serum bicarbonate and anion gap prior to therapy initiation, followed by periodic electrolyte and acid base evaluation during treatment, particularly among dialysis-dependent patients. Therapy reassessment or dose adjustment should be considered in patients demonstrating progressive anion gap elevation or declining serum bicarbonate levels. Routine monitoring of acid–base parameters and heightened clinical awareness are essential. Future prospective studies are urgently required to define the true incidence, risk factors, and clinical consequences of STS-induced metabolic acidosis, thereby optimizing patient safety while preserving potential therapeutic benefit. title: Haptic-feedback robotics in transcervical fetal endoscopy: reducing uterine irritability and the risk of preterm labor
abstract: To the Editor, Infants are born preterm at less than 37 weeks’ gestational age. Recently, the rate of preterm birth has increased in many places. Common reasons for indicated preterm births include pre-eclampsia or eclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction. Births that follow spontaneous preterm labor and preterm prelabor rupture of membranes are regarded as a syndrome resulting from multiple causes, including infection or inflammation[1]. The incidence of preterm labor in women with uterine irritability is not as frequent as in patients with other high-risk factors. However, preterm labor appears to occur in patients with uterine irritability at a rate higher than that in the general obstetric population (18.7 vs. 11%). Because it seems that women with uterine irritability have more resistance to tocolytic therapy, this condition should prompt the physician to use more aggressive perinatal assessment[2]. Haptic-feedback robotics refers to automated surgical devices that provide haptic cues to the surgeon, designed to enhance precision during particular procedures. In minimally invasive surgery, including scope-based interventions, haptic feedback improves tactile awareness that is undetectable by surgical tools. Robotic systems equipped with haptic interfaces work by detecting contact pressures between the instrument tip and organ material and transforming them into kinesthetic or tactile cues at the surgeon’s control console[3]. Hypothetically, haptic-augmented robots could limit uterine irritability during transcervical fetal endoscopy by enabling careful force application, lessening myometrium excitation that triggers premature labor. The functional mechanism involves force/torque sensors on the instrument tip, relayed back to the operator console, allowing the surgeon to “feel” tissue resistance[4]. Studies on haptic-feedback robotics in minimally invasive surgery show improved accuracy and reduced injury[5]. In laparoscopic trials, surgeons using tactile-assisted control lowered tool pressure by 20–30%, reducing tissue trauma and collisions[3]. Although clinical evidence for transcervical fetal endoscopy is limited, comparable techniques may reduce myometrial contractions and the risk of premature delivery. Risk assessments were favorable, with no complications, and most cases showed enhanced postoperative outcomes. Generally, haptic guidance efficiently lowers surgical mistakes and tissue injury, supporting its future implementation in fetal surgery. The most significant barrier limiting the use of haptic robotics for fetal endoscopy is the financial toll it takes on resources. These systems present high costs for both initial installation and later maintenance[6]. In addition, the use of complex robotic interfaces can potentially delay intervention in case of an emergency. Miniaturized instruments are required for safe fetal access and for preventing preterm labor, which can lead to technical challenges. Furthermore, these long instruments can create friction and noise, interfering with the haptic cues the surgeon receives. These limitations make haptic robotics for fetal endoscopy and other surgical procedures a process that requires further development and finesse before it can be considered completely trustworthy[7]. The use of haptic-feedback robotics in transcervical fetal endoscopy is an important step toward low-risk surgeries for intrauterine pathologies. This system has the ability to significantly diminish the chance of myometrial hyperactivity and resulting preterm labor. The field must aim to guarantee the effective incorporation of this innovation. Extensive, collaborative randomized controlled trials are required immediately to precisely measure the findings. Upcoming research and development ought to focus on minimizing present haptic system barriers by refining force-feedback clarity, incorporating reliable tactile sensing, and miniaturizing instruments to limit trauma. Simulation training protocols with haptic feedback help us quickly and safely pass on surgical expertise. It is also important that these programs remain cost-effective. This letter to the editor adheres to the Transparency in the Reporting of Artificial Intelligence in Research (TITAN) guideline[8].

title: A decade without updated information on radiology in Nepal: an alarming situation
abstract: Dear Editor, I am writing to express my concerns regarding the severe lack of studies and information in Nepal’s radiology field. We read the article by Subedi Sharma1 with great attention, which reflects the scenario of infrastructure and manpower in radiology in Nepal in 2012. Unfortunately, no studies have been conducted with updated information on radiology in Nepal for more than a decade. Without a thorough understanding of the existing resources, infrastructure, and challenges, it becomes difficult to identify loopholes, allocate resources, and ensure equitable distribution of these vital facilities in Nepal’s struggling health system. The study reported 150 radiologists and 350 radiographers, portraying a ratio of 1 radiologist per 200,000 population in 2012. The available equipment included a few pieces of radiotherapy equipment, 10 magnetic resonance imaging scanners, 30 computed tomography (CT) scanners, 11 mammographic scanners, 1200 x-ray machines, and 800 ultrasound machines. While there have been certain advances in the number of skilled manpower and infrastructure, an increase in the interest of medical students in radiology, and the introduction of interventional radiology, the literature has not been updated with the latest numbers, the beginning of PET-CT services and facilities like mechanical thrombectomy, increased residency spots in radiology, and other advancements. Nepal is a low-income country in the lap of the Himalayas, facing geographic as well as socio-economic and political challenges. With a per capita income of US$10342, the total health care expenditure accounts for 5.5% of the government’s total budget1. A perspective by Brant et al3 takes us back to the 1990s when radiology had just started in Nepal. It was available in a few hospitals in Kathmandu. While plain radiography and sonography were the main tools, a few interventional procedures, nuclear medicine, and radiotherapy were also available. A 2-year training program for a diploma in medical radiologic diagnosis was the fast track to address the shortage of radiologists. However, even after 3 decades, when the world of radiology is partnering with artificial intelligence, many hospitals in Nepal still use conventional radiology equipment, some up to 20 years old1. For instance, rural hospitals provide services with small x-ray units powered by electric generators and manual film development1,4,5. The infrastructure and manpower show significantly uneven distribution between major cities and the rest of the country1,4. The irony is that there is a paucity of literature on the availability of types of radiology services, their distribution by demographics and geography, and the prevailing obstacles. To address this alarming shortage of information on the current state of radiodiagnostics in Nepal, comprehensive studies must be undertaken to assess its current status and gradual transition. This research will provide critical insights into the existing infrastructure, resource gaps, and areas needing improvement. Furthermore, existing bodies like the Nepal Radiologists’ Association (NRA), Nepal Radiological Society (NRS), etc., should be committed to monitoring and maintaining the integrity of quality radiology services and continuously keeping records of all updates. All governmental and nongovernmental organizations should collaborate together leveraging their network and support and a centralized database should be established to track the number and distribution of USG, CT, magnetic resonance imaging, and PET machines across Nepal. title: The unforeseen consequence of smart bio-implants for hemophilia: chronic inflammation and antibody development
abstract: Dear Editor, Hemophilia is an inherited (X-linked recessive) bleeding disorder characterized by impaired blood coagulation. The pathogenesis of hemophilia involves a hereditary deficiency of blood-clotting factor VIII (Type A hemophilia) or IX (Type B hemophilia) that disrupts secondary hemostasis[1]. Globally, factor VIII deficiency is present in approximately 1 in 5000–10 000 males at birth, whereas factor IX deficiency occurs in around 1 in 40,000 males. Accurate diagnosis of hemophilia relies on laboratory evaluations, including prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), specific coagulation factor assays to determine activity levels, and confirmatory genetic testing to identify underlying mutations. Current management of hemophilia includes conventional clotting factor replacement therapy, non-factor agents such as monoclonal antibodies, and novel smart bio-implantable systems, collectively aimed at reducing bleeding frequency[2]. Smart bio-implants are an emerging therapeutic approach being studied as an intervention for chronic diseases such as diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular disorders, and hemophilia. These implants integrate biosensors and drug reservoirs with biocompatible microelectromechanical components (MEMS) to monitor physiological signals and deliver medication when required. For hemophilia, bio-implants aim to provide persistent factor delivery and continuous monitoring, which could mitigate bleeding episodes and lessen the therapeutic load compared to conventional infusions[3,4]. Despite proposed benefits, multiple challenges limit the clinical use of smart bio-implants in hemophilia. The foremost concern remains the risk of the development of chronic inflammation and immunogenicity. The implantation of smart bio-devices triggers “foreign body reaction,” initiated by nonspecific protein deposition onto the implant surface, followed by migration and activation of innate immune cells such as neutrophils and macrophages. Macrophage activation and cellular fusion into foreign-body giant cells (FBGCs) induce the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reactive oxygen species, and profibrotic mediators, leading to chronic inflammation and scar tissue formation surrounding the implant. This prolonged inflammation may serve as an immune-stimulating factor, enhancing antigen presentation and promoting the activation of adaptive immune pathways (B- and T-cell mediated immunity). In patients with hemophilia, such immune stimulation poses a risk for antibody (inhibitor) development against therapeutic clotting factors, potentially reducing factor activity and worsening bleeding control. Beyond inhibitor formation, this immune response may also compromise implant viability, shorten device lifespan, and ultimately undermine long-term therapeutic outcomes in hemophilia management[5,6]. Furthermore, there is a limited availability of hemophilia-specific preclinical and clinical studies, as most evidence regarding implantable biosystems is extrapolated from other chronic diseases. Also, high costs, surgical implantation requirements, and device management difficulties limit accessibility and patient acceptance. Additional limitations include insufficient healthcare provider and patient awareness, unresolved concerns regarding long-term device performance, and the lack of standardized regulatory guidelines. Collectively, these challenges highlight the need for applied clinical research evaluating immunologic safety, cost-effectiveness, and long-term outcomes before large-scale implementation in the management of hemophilia[7]. In conclusion, despite the fact that smart bio-implants offer promising advances in hemophilia management, their potential is limited by risks of chronic inflammation and antibody development. Future strategies should prioritize hemophilia-specific clinical trials and structural modifications to improve biocompatibility and long-term performance. At the same time, healthcare providers’ and patients’ awareness about immunologic risks and correct implant utilization is necessary to ensure that this intervention leads to safe and effective clinical outcomes. This letter to the editor adheres to the Transparency in the Reporting of Artificial Intelligence in Research (TITAN) guideline[8].

title: Beyond antifungals: vaginal ceramides as a barrier-restorative strategy for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
abstract: To the Editor, Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (RVVC) is a chronic and irritating disease characterized by three or more symptomatic occurrences of vulvovaginal candidiasis in a year. It is a condition that severely undermines women’s physical, sexual, and psychological health. The majority of infected women fall into the reproductive age group, with a median of 29 years, and the main causative agent is Candida albicans, which accounts for 92.5% of isolates, followed by Candida lusitaniae at 7.5%. The difficulty in managing the infection is compounded by the emergence of azole-resistant strains, which leads to recurring and sometimes permanent infections. Immunology-based studies demonstrate that women suffering from RVVC exhibit less neutrophil activity and have C. albicans immune responses that differ from the normal ones, thus making it clear that the infection has a multifactorial nature and is a large health problem worldwide[1]. RVVC is further complicated in patients with Ehler-Danlos syndrome (EDS), a heterogeneous group of connective tissue disorders, where varying degrees of tissue fragility and impaired barrier function may lead to recurrent infections[2], underscoring the therapeutic potential of vaginal ceramides to improve vaginal defense and the integrity of the vulvovaginal epithelial barrier. Candida adherence and colonization in the vagina are normally balanced by host immunity and microbiota; however, factors like impaired innate immune responses disrupt this homeostasis, leading to recurrent infections[3]. Recent clinical studies indicate that EDS is associated with serious urogenital complications, including vaginal dryness, genital fissures, and recurrent vaginal infections, which are largely due to underlying collagen defects[2]. Such a connective tissue integrity defect may lead to a fragile vulvovaginal epithelium, facilitating Candida adherence and immune dysregulation, and predisposing to recurrence of vulvovaginal candidiasis. Emerging clinical findings show that ceramides are an essential component of the lipid barrier of both skin and mucosa, playing a key role in maintaining barrier integrity and defending against pathogens, suggesting a novel approach for preventing RVVC in EDS[4]. Current RVVC management depends on antifungal azoles like fluconazole. However, increasing resistance and limited long-term efficacy remain major challenges in continued treatment. One of the key contributors to this antifungal resistance is biofilm formation by Candida, which promotes recurrence and increases drug tolerance[5]. Newer agents such as oteseconazole and ibrexafungerp show promising results in light of these challenges; their use is limited by safety and availability issues, while vaccines like NDV-3A are still under study. Notably, existing strategies widely neglect mucosal barrier integrity, critical in EDS, which highlights the need to switch from antimicrobial therapy alone toward barrier restoration interventions, such as ceramides[6]. Despite the theoretical promise of vaginal ceramides, several important clinical limitations need to be addressed. First, no direct clinical evidence for vaginal ceramide therapy in women with EDS was found, with subtype-related mucosal heterogeneity potentially impacting treatment outcomes, safety, and generalizability[2]. Moreover, most ceramide research has concentrated on skin, which has left the vulvovaginal mucosal barrier largely uncharacterized; due to this, its tolerability in non-cutaneous environments and long-term efficacy remain unclear[3]. Finally, the combined effect of specific ceramide formulations with existing antifungals and their long-term influence on recurrence and vaginal mucosal health requires thorough investigation. The case of RVVC in EDS highlights a major drawback of nowadays azole-centric approaches, since the combination of collagen-induced weakness in the epithelium with Candida biofilm and immune dysregulation already requires not just the microbial suppression but also some other methods of intervention[1,2,5]. Vaginal ceramides, by restoring the mucosal lipid barriers, can directly prevent the pathogens from adhering to the cells, and at the same time, the tissue integrity gets damaged in this segment of the population, thus replacing a mechanistic gap that has not been covered by the new agents oteseconazole or ibrexafungerp[4,6]. There is an urgent need for clinicians to initiate subtype-stratified trials that combine ceramides with antifungals to determine tolerability and recurrence endpoints in EDS[2]; investigators must explore ceramide distribution and longevity in vulvovaginal mucosa compared to cutaneous models[3,4]; and stakeholders should financially support prospective cohorts that assess barrier function, biofilm burden, and patient-reported outcomes to validate this adjunctive, barrier-restorative strategy[5,6]. In summary, the novel use of vaginal ceramides for managing RVVC represents a physiologically sound, patient-centric, and mechanism-based adjunct to current therapies aiming to restore barrier integrity and decrease susceptibility to infection. This barrier repair approach revolutionizes RVVC treatment in EDS patients, where barrier dysfunction and immune modulation may potentiate recurrence, which cannot be managed by conventional antifungal therapy alone. Through further research, optimizing formulations, and safe dosing regimens, a multifaceted approach has the potential to fill a significant gap in current management with the ultimate goal of improving quality of life. This letter to the editor adheres to the Transparency in the Reporting of Artificial Intelligence in Research (TITAN) guideline[7]. During the preparation of this manuscript, generative AI tools (DeepSeek, DeepSeek Inc., June 2025 version; temperature parameter = 0.7) were used only as auxiliary aids to assist in formatting standardization, organization of background information, and language consistency checks. All AI-assisted text was thoroughly reviewed, edited, and refined by the authors. The conceptualization, literature interpretation, synthesis of ideas, and manuscript writing were performed entirely by the authors, ensuring the academic rigor, accuracy, and originality of the review.

title: Putting technology between people and tigers
abstract: In 2010, during a St. Petersburg summit on tigers, 13 tiger range countries agreed to double the global tiger population by 2022. As a result, long-term coordinated efforts have been implemented to recover tiger populations, including controlling the illegal trade of tigers, protecting and restoring habitat and movement corridors, and patrolling against poaching. Local people have been pivotal to tiger conservation efforts across the tiger range states (Wikramanayake et al., 2010). An estimated 1737 tigers have been added to the global tiger population since 2010 in four of the 13 tiger range countries (i.e. India, Nepal, Russia, and Bhutan; Supporting Information). These gains are good news for tiger conservation, but they risk being undermined if the potential for increased human-tiger conflict is not managed (Acharya et al., 2016). Deaths and injuries due to tiger attacks are at a high level in several countries (Supporting Information). Much of the tiger habitat in South Asia is close to areas with the highest human population densities in the world, coupled with high population growth and rapid urbanization (CIESIN, 2018). As tigers require large areas, with growing human and tiger populations, it is anticipated that there could be greater potential for conflict. Management of tigers that are dangerous to human life requires the identification, capture, and rehabilitation of problem individuals, which is often difficult, time-consuming, and expensive. Identification of such animals requires the deployment of intensive camera trap arrays (NTCA, 2013), and often manual retrieval and processing of data. Furthermore, such animals may mix with non-problem ones, making the differentiation between the two lengthy and complex process (NTCA, 2013). Lengthy delays between reporting and capture of animals increase the chances of further escalation of conflicts. Other methods like electric fencing, to prevent trespassing, can be expensive, insufficient, and are often fatal to tigers (The Hindu, 2017). Governments have implemented compensation payments in several countries to provide economic support to victims' families and to garner positive attitudes toward tigers and their conservation (Karanth, Gupta & Vanamamalai, 2018; DNPWC, 2019). This is, however, often too slow due to a lag in communication and bureaucratic processes (Karanth, Gupta & Vanamamalai, 2018), and clearly is inadequate for proactively mitigating conflicts. We believe new technology offers great potential for reducing human-tiger conflicts. For example, automated systems integrating high-resolution imaging sensors, wireless technology, and artificial intelligence (AI) (Norouzzadeh et al., 2018) could be used to rapidly detect, identify, track, and warn of tiger presence. These systems enable real-time data processing and notification capabilities, thus significantly reducing time lags in detection and action. They can also be useful for helping managers to forecast and respond immediately and effectively. Developments of such systems are already taking place. For example, a mobile sensor to capture images, AI to detect and identify animals from the images, and transmission of information over a mobile network to warn of animal presence show great potential for mitigating human-elephant conflict in Thailand (Mongabay, 2020). In addition, a centralized mobile application that allows local community members to submit information on tiger presence and behavior could have great potential in reducing conflicts. Mobile applications would make it convenient to report, communicate, and track conflicts and compensation, such as the open-source technology Wild Seve used in India (Karanth & Vanamamalai, 2020). Other technologies such as non-imaging sensors (Kamminga et al., 2018) can also be used to notify of tiger intrusions. Such systems could be cheaper, cover large areas, and provide real-time warnings, giving locals a chance to prepare and respond. Non-lethal deterrents such as fox lights to deter leopards in India (Naha et al., 2020), pumas in Chile (Ohrens, Bonacic & Treves, 2019), ultrasonic repellents to deter cats in Australia (Crawford, Fontaine & Calver, 2018), and LED flashlights in Kenya to deter lions (Lesilau et al., 2018), may also be a promising approach to tiger conflict management. Currently, such technologies are underutilized in South Asia. This could be due to the high costs involved with implementing new infrastructure and training personnel, reluctance to adopt new technology or a perceived uncertainty in its effectiveness. Investment to prevent and mitigate conflicts through the application of new technology is likely to be far more cost effective than traditional approaches. If tiger range countries collaborate on research and development, technology deployment costs could be significantly reduced. New knowledge integration and local employment opportunities would be an added advantage. While increasing tiger populations is of utmost importance, this should not come at the expense of human life in the tiger range countries. Greater efforts to research and test proactive technologies are needed to help people live alongside tigers and to maintain their support for tiger conservation. We believe building and testing systems using shared databases within cloud computing frameworks to implement analytics, prediction, and data mining offer great potential for preventing and mitigating conflicts. title: Needle stick injuries: a cause for concern
abstract: Needle stick injury (NSI) represents a significant occupational risk for hospital professionals[1]. It is among the most serious risks to HCWs safety in the modern healthcare systems[2]. Any sharp object can induce NSIs, which include injuries from contact with hypodermic needles, venepuncture needle, cannulas, and needles used to connect intravenous administration system components, among other things. NSIs, also referred to as NSIs, are wounds brought on by sharp objects or possibly contaminated needles[3]. NSIs were present in 56.2% of HCWs worldwide over the course of their careers. Out of the 35 million HCWs, the WHO forecasts that 3 million are exposed to NSI on each year[4]. NSI prevalence is highest in Southeast Asia and Africa, while the Western Pacific region has the lowest. The United States of America reported the lowest prevalence at 25.1%, while Southeast Asia experienced the highest prevalence at 49.9%. Furthermore, developed countries (30.5%) and developing countries (46.6%) differ from each other, with low-middle sustainable development index (SDI) countries possessing the highest NSI prevalence (48.9%). In nations with stronger economies, the incidence of NSI is lower[5]. NSI prevalence is higher in underdeveloped nations compared to developed nations. Still, projections of frequency in Pakistan that is 77% followed by Iran and India that is 76% and 68%, were remarkably high. NSIs are the cause of 39% of HCV, 37% of HBV, and 4.5% of HIV infections in HCWs. The implementation of extensive hospital-level NSI prevention programs, the creation of training programs, the availability of reliable information regarding NSI management, the placing NSI cases as an urgent issue, and the formation of a preventive perspective on NSIs among nurses are all factors that contribute to the low NSI prevalence in developed nations. Lack of staff and NSI incidents, on the other hand, can be blamed for the high prevalence of NSI in developing nations. In units with sufficient staff, there has been a reported twofold increase in NSI. The unusually high frequency in underdeveloped countries was caused by inadequate personal protective equipment (PPE) and an inadequacy of training on Hospital infection prevention and control. Viral infections such as hepatitis B and hepatitis C comprise 37% to 39% of NSIs, adversely affecting the quality of life of HCWs[6,7].The chances of contracting HBV, HCV, or HIV from a single exposure to blood contaminated with viruses are 6-30%, 0-7%, and 0.2-0.5%, respectively. Among the contact injuries, cutaneous injury caused by NSI has a higher stake, with a prevalence of 35.3%. A significant rise in anxiety scores has been associated with post-exposure to NSIs among the HCWs[6]. NSI is a stressful state manifesting commonly in terms of emotional exhaustion and stress[5]. It is problematic when it comes to high-risk patients who test positive for HIV and HCV, as these conditions can have a detrimental effect on mental health and are thought to be responsible for a high prevalence of stress and depression in healthcare workers, ranging from 42% to 60%[5]. Around 3.2% and 0.9% of HBV and HCV infections are reported among nurses as an adverse effect of NSIs[6]. According to the WHO, engineering variables, institutional, administrative factors (like supply availability), and behavioral factors—mostly pertaining to concerns about the disposal of needles and sharps can all be broadly linked to the occurrence of NSIs. These factors also include the level of training, knowledge and skills within healthcare workers[6]. More than half of the NSIs globally are associated with hypodermic needles, followed by IV cannula (23%) and needle sutures (19.6%)[5].Various literature states a significant burden associated with insulin injection-induced NSI among the HCWs of the Asia-Pacific region. PPE, practice of recapping needles, longer working hours, posting in emergency and operating units, and lack of knowledge and skills regarding infection prevention and control measures contribute to increased incidences of NSI. NSI is also associated with hospital crowding, inadequate nurse-to-patient ratio, inadequacy in appropriate safety equipment, and failure to adopt precautions[6]. Recapping the needle forcefully or segregating the syringes or needles without proper precautionary practices are known causes of NSIs in the past. Some of the studies reflect the HCWs’ assumptions for recapping the needles after use (66.1%), and only 52.5% are aware of the practices regarding needleless safety devices[6]. The medical and surgical departments have witnessed over 50% of the NSI incidence, with the operating room (3%), trauma and emergency rooms (38%). One of the most common procedures increasing the incidences of NSI is insulin administration among the diabetic population[4]. Emergency unit personnel, surgeons, and nurses are particularly vulnerable to NSI. Globally, the prevalence of NSI among nurses is approximately 41%, whereas among nursing students, it ranges from 8.7% to 71%[6]. According to estimates, that percentage is 45.3% for nursing students, 46.4% for doctors, and 42.8% for nurses[4]. The risk of blood-borne pathogen transmission results in considerable mortality; however, there is little reporting of NSI occurrence. According to a report by the Centre for Disease Control (CDC), barely half of the 3,85,000 instances of NSI were recorded. Nurses fail to report NSI for a variety of reasons, such as forgetting about the incidence, being too busy, not understanding the risk, being afraid of reactive serological diagnostic tests, and lacking the necessary skills[2]. Because of inadequate preventive measures to combat NSI, HCWs suffer approximately 80,000 infections annually across the globe[5].Standard precautions must be used while dealing with potentially infectious fluids, mostly involving blood and blood components. In order to lower the number of NSI cases, develop and enhance the professional identification and tracking system following a high-risk exposure, follow suggested hours of work, include professional safety programs in the curriculum, and guarantee that the necessary equipment is available. Health care authorities are recommended to plan regular training programs to prevent NSI in HCWs. The periodic evaluation of HCWs should assess the skills generated by training programs and the uniformity of policy implementation across the healthcare sector in managing NSI. Despite existing strategies, there is a need to develop sustainable solutions incorporating artificial intelligence into the current practices for the effective management of NSI in both developed and developing countries.
